en: Created for a particular purpose only, not planned in advance
hook: AD HOC: Latin for 'for this' — for this one purpose only.
story: Ad hoc. When floodwater suddenly poured into the ground floor of a hospital in Sylhet, there was no plan for it. Doctors, cleaners, and patients' relatives formed an ad hoc team on the spot, passing beds and medicine boxes upstairs in a human chain. Ad hoc means created for one particular purpose only, not planned in advance. The Latin literally means for this. An ad hoc committee dissolves when its task is done. Contrast systematic. Synonyms: improvised, impromptu, makeshift.

gre.s: Rather than developing a coherent policy, the ministry responded to each crisis in a purely ____ fashion, devising quick fixes that were abandoned once the emergency passed.
gre.clue: Rather than developing a coherent policy

example: Without a written schedule, the volunteers at the book fair relied on ad hoc arrangements, deciding each morning who would staff which stall.

en: To permit; also, to admit or concede that something is true
hook: GRE trick: ALLOW can mean ADMIT — 'he allowed that he was wrong.'
story: Allow. Rafi and his sister Nadia argued for an hour about whether Messi or Ronaldo was the greater player. Rafi refused to give an inch, until Nadia pulled up the statistics on her phone. Rafi sighed. "All right, I will allow that Messi has more assists," he said, "but Ronaldo is better in big matches." Here, to allow means to admit or concede that something is true. Its everyday meaning is to permit, as when parents allow a trip. Synonyms: concede, grant, acknowledge.

gre.s: Even her harshest critics would ____ that her research was meticulous, though they continued to dispute the conclusions she drew from it.
gre.clue: though they continued to dispute the conclusions

example: The referee later allowed that the goal might have been offside, though he insisted he had no clear view at the time.

en: Suitable or proper for the situation (adj.); to take something for one's own use, often without permission (verb)
hook: Two pronunciations: ap-PRO-pree-it means SUITABLE; ap-PRO-pree-ate means to TAKE as your PROPERTY.
story: Appropriate. Rafi spent a month designing a poster for the university festival. A week later, a senior student printed it with his own name at the bottom. He had appropriated Rafi's work: taken it for his own use without permission. That verb is a GRE favourite. As an adjective, appropriate simply means suitable, like appropriate clothes for an interview. Governments also appropriate funds, setting money aside for a particular purpose. Synonyms for the verb: seize, commandeer, usurp.

gre.s: Critics accused the fashion house of choosing to ____ traditional Jamdani motifs for its new collection without ever crediting the weavers who had developed them over centuries.
gre.clue: without ever crediting the weavers

example: During the war, the army appropriated several private villas in the hills and turned them into field hospitals.

en: Respected and impressive; majestic
hook: GRE trick: au-GUST, like Emperor AUGUSTUS, majestic.
story: August. When the eighty-year-old chief justice entered the hall in his black robes, white-haired and upright, every lawyer rose in silence. Even the noisiest journalists lowered their voices. His presence was august: respected and impressive, majestic. Note the stress, aw-GUST, unlike the month. Both come from Augustus, the Roman emperor whose title meant venerable. An august institution, like an ancient university, inspires awe. Synonyms: venerable, dignified, stately.

gre.s: The young scholar felt intimidated in the ____ company of Nobel laureates and former heads of state, and barely dared to speak during the entire dinner.
gre.clue: Nobel laureates and former heads of state

example: The journal, founded in 1887, is one of the most august publications in the field, and acceptance there can make a young chemist's career.

en: Shamefully dishonorable and selfish, lacking any moral decency
hook: GRE trick: BASE means LOW morally, like the bottom of a building.
story: Base. During a flood, a shopkeeper in Sunamganj hoarded rice and sold it to hungry families at three times the normal price. When a relief volunteer pleaded with him, he laughed and raised the price again. The villagers called his behaviour base: morally low, without principles or dignity. This base has nothing to do with a foundation. Think of debased, meaning lowered in value. Base motives include greed, cowardice, and spite. Synonyms: ignoble, vile, contemptible. Opposite: noble.

gre.s: Investigators concluded that the official had acted from the most ____ motives, since he had accepted bribes to approve a dam he knew was unsafe.
gre.clue: accepted bribes to approve a dam he knew was unsafe

example: Spreading false rumors about a rival candidate's family was a base tactic, and even his own supporters were ashamed of it.

en: To publicly support or fight for a cause
hook: GRE trick: to CHAMPION a cause means to fight FOR it.
story: Champion. When the local council planned to fill in an old pond in Mymensingh to build a market, a retired schoolteacher named Rumana refused to stay quiet. She wrote letters to newspapers, organised students, and spoke at every public meeting. Thanks to her, the pond survived. She had championed its cause: publicly supported and fought for it. As a verb, to champion means to defend a cause, not to win a trophy. Synonyms: advocate, espouse, defend.

gre.s: Though she was initially skeptical of renewable energy, the senator went on to ____ it more vigorously than any of her colleagues, sponsoring dozens of bills to expand solar power.
gre.clue: sponsoring dozens of bills to expand solar power

example: The young librarian championed a reading program for street children in Kamalapur, persuading local businesses to donate books and snacks.

en: Belonging to the same period as another; also, of the present day
hook: CON-TEMPORARY: with (con) the same time (tempus).
story: Contemporary. Rabindranath Tagore and Albert Einstein met near Berlin in 1930 and talked about science and truth. They were contemporaries: people living at the same time. A history student writing about the meeting would look for contemporary accounts, written by people alive then. But in an art gallery, contemporary means modern, of the present day, as in contemporary art. Con means together and tempus means time. Context tells you which sense. Synonyms: concurrent, coeval; or modern, current.

gre.s: Historians prefer ____ accounts of the battle, written by eyewitnesses, to the romanticized versions that poets composed a full century later.
gre.clue: written by eyewitnesses

example: Shakespeare and Cervantes were contemporary writers, and the two men died within days of each other in the spring of 1616.

en: Peacefully satisfied
hook: CON-TENT (stress on TENT): happy in your little tent.
story: Content. Rahim, a boatman on the Meghna, owns one wooden boat, a tin-roofed house, and three goats. Each evening he sits by the river with a cup of tea and watches the sunset. When a visitor from the city asked whether he wanted more, he laughed. "What more? I have enough." He is content: peacefully satisfied with what he has. Stress the second syllable, con-TENT. Do not confuse it with CON-tent, what something contains. Synonyms: satisfied, serene.

gre.s: Unlike her restless siblings, who constantly chased new ventures, she was ____ with the quiet life of a village schoolteacher and never sought promotion.
gre.clue: Unlike her restless siblings, who constantly chased new ventures

example: After years of chasing promotions in Dhaka, Kamal was finally content to run a small guesthouse among the tea gardens of Srimangal.

en: Following accepted customs and standards; traditional
hook: CONVENTIONAL: what everyone agreed on at the CONVENTION.
story: Conventional. Rafi's parents had a plan for him: doctor, engineer, or a government job. Safe. Respected. Ordinary. At the family dinner, Rafi announced he wanted to be a wildlife photographer in the Sundarbans. His uncle choked on his rice. "That is not a real job!" Conventional means following traditional, widely accepted customs and standards. Conventional wisdom is what most people believe. GRE passages often describe a researcher who challenges conventional assumptions.

gre.s: Defying ____ wisdom, which held that the disease was inherited, the researcher argued that it was caused by an environmental toxin.
gre.clue: which held that the disease was inherited

example: The architect rejected the conventional glass tower and designed an office block wrapped in screens of living bamboo.

en: To regard as unimportant or untrustworthy; to disregard
hook: GRE trick: DISCOUNT means to ignore, not just lower the price.
story: Discount. Mitu's grandmother has diabetes. When a neighbour insisted that bitter lemon water could replace her insulin, the doctor did not argue. He simply discounted the advice and kept her on her medicine. Some claims deserve to be discounted: regarded as unimportant or untrustworthy, and set aside. In a shop, a discount reduces the price; in an argument, discounting a claim reduces its weight to almost nothing. Never discount a theory just because it is new. Synonyms: disregard, dismiss.

gre.s: Scientists were quick to ____ the anonymous report, since its author offered no data and had a long history of fabricating results.
gre.clue: had a long history of fabricating results

example: Coach Habib discounted the injury rumors and named his striker in the starting eleven for the final.

en: Consisting of or based on real documents or facts
hook: DOCUMENTARY: backed by DOCUMENTS.
story: Documentary. A historian claimed that a famous zamindar's palace had once been a hospital during the 1943 famine. Other scholars doubted her. Then she presented her proof: hospital registers, letters, government orders, and photographs, all dated 1943. Her evidence was documentary: based on real documents and records. As an adjective, documentary means consisting of factual records. A documentary film presents real events rather than fiction.

gre.s: The historian's claims rest on solid ____ evidence, including letters, ledgers, and court records from the period.
gre.clue: including letters, ledgers, and court records

example: No documentary proof of the land sale survived the fire, so the court had to rely on the testimony of elderly villagers.

en: Using money, effort or words sparingly and without waste
hook: GRE trick: ECONOMY of words means using no more words than needed.
story: Economy. Every month Sara's mother received a small salary, yet the family never went short. She bought vegetables in season, used cooking oil carefully, and turned leftover rice into breakfast. Her neighbours admired her economy: careful management of resources, wasting nothing. On the GRE, economy often describes style, too. A writer with economy of language never uses ten words when three will do. So economy means thrift and efficiency, not only a nation's finances. Synonyms: thrift, frugality, efficiency.

gre.s: Her prose is admired for its remarkable ____: she never uses three words where one will do, and every sentence seems to earn its place.
gre.clue: she never uses three words where one will do

example: With remarkable economy of movement, the old carpenter smoothed the plank in a few strokes while his apprentice watched in silence.

en: Basic; relating to the simplest beginning stages
hook: ELEMENTARY: the basic ELEMENTS.
story: Elementary. On the first day of the GRE quant course, Arif felt almost insulted. The teacher began with fractions, percentages, and the area of a triangle, things he had learned in class six. But the teacher explained that elementary ideas are the foundation for everything harder. Elementary means basic, relating to the simplest beginning stages. An elementary school teaches the first steps of learning, and an elementary mistake is one even a beginner should avoid. Synonyms: basic, rudimentary, fundamental.

gre.s: Although the textbook advertises itself as an advanced treatment of the subject, its exercises are so ____ that a first-year student could finish them in an afternoon.
gre.clue: a first-year student could finish them in an afternoon

example: The first experiment in the chemistry lab was elementary, just timing how quickly salt dissolves in warm and cold water.

en: Feeling owed special treatment that one has not earned
bn: নিজেকে বিশেষ সুবিধার যোগ্য মনে করে এমন; অধিকারবোধসম্পন্ন
hook: ENTITLED: acts like he holds a royal TITLE.
story: Entitled. At the university canteen, a long queue waited for lunch. A student in designer sunglasses walked straight to the front and said, "Do you know who my father is?" He expected the rules not to apply to him. Nobody moved for him, and the cashier pointed to the back of the line. His attitude was entitled: believing he deserved special treatment without earning it. In law, you can also be legally entitled to a right.

gre.s: The coach was frustrated by the star player's ____ attitude, as he expected special privileges while skipping the practices everyone else attended.
gre.clue: expected special privileges

example: The entitled customer at the Gulshan restaurant demanded a free dessert simply because he had waited five minutes for his table.

en: Natural ease or skill in doing something
hook: GRE trick: FACILITY means ease — she has a facility for languages.
story: Facility. Joya's little brother has never taken a single music lesson, yet he can hear a song once on the radio and play it on the harmonium straight away. His teachers are amazed by his facility with melody: a natural ease and skill in doing something. The word is related to facile and facilitate, all from the Latin for easy. Facility also means a building, like a sports facility, but the GRE prefers the ease sense. Synonyms: aptitude, fluency, knack.

gre.s: Despite her obvious ____ with languages, which allowed her to pick up conversational Italian in a matter of weeks, she struggled for years with basic arithmetic.
gre.clue: pick up conversational Italian in a matter of weeks

example: Rafsan's facility with numbers made him the person everyone called whenever the family's tax forms had to be filled in.

en: Open, honest, and direct
hook: FRANK: Frank always tells it straight.
story: Frank. When Shuvo asked his mentor to read his first short story, he hoped for praise. Instead she said, "The opening is dull, the dialogue is stiff, and the ending is borrowed. But the third page is brilliant; build from there." It stung, but it helped. She was frank: open, honest, and direct. Frank once meant free, from the Franks, a free people; frank speech is free of disguise. Synonyms: candid, blunt, forthright.

gre.s: Rather than offering the vague reassurances his patients expected, the doctor was always ____, telling them plainly what their prognosis was even when the news was grim.
gre.clue: telling them plainly what their prognosis was

example: In a frank interview, the retired captain admitted that his team had been badly unprepared for the tour of Australia.

en: Extremely small; precise and detailed (pronounced my-NOOT)
hook: MINUTE (my-NOOT): as tiny as a MINI thing.
story: Minute. In a forensic lab, Doctor Joya examined a minute speck of blood on a shirt cuff, so tiny it was invisible to the naked eye. Her report described it with minute care, down to its exact position on a single thread. Pronounced my-noot, minute means extremely small, or precise and detailed. Do not confuse it with the minute on a clock. Minute, minuscule, and diminish share a root meaning small. Synonyms: tiny, infinitesimal, meticulous. Opposite: enormous.

gre.s: Although the changes to the manuscript appeared ____, they altered the meaning of several key passages in ways that scholars still debate.
gre.clue: they altered the meaning of several key passages

example: Engineers found that a minute crack in a turbine blade, thinner than a hair, had caused the entire engine to fail.

en: Having high moral qualities; aristocratic
hook: NOBLE: like a NOBEL Prize-worthy character.
story: Noble. A rickshaw puller in Dhaka found a bag containing two lakh taka under his seat. He was poor, and his daughter needed school fees. Still, he spent the whole day searching until he found the owner, returned every note, and refused any reward. The newspapers called his act noble: showing high moral qualities. Noble also means aristocratic, as in a noble family, but the GRE usually wants the moral sense. Synonyms: honourable, virtuous, magnanimous. Opposite: base.

gre.s: Although she could easily have kept the reward for herself, she made the ____ choice to donate it to the families of the miners who had died.
gre.clue: Although she could easily have kept the reward for herself

example: Giving up his own scholarship so that his younger sister could study abroad was a noble sacrifice, though Nayeem never spoke of it.

en: Easily shaped or molded; flexible and adaptable
hook: GRE trick: PLASTIC means moldable, like clay — not just the material.
story: Plastic. Neuroscientists say a child's brain is plastic: it rewires itself constantly, learns languages easily, and can even recover after an injury by sending signals along new paths. On the GRE, plastic rarely means a shopping bag. It means moldable, flexible, and able to be shaped. Clay is plastic; stone is not. Plastic surgery originally meant surgery that reshapes the body. Plastic arts, like sculpture, shape material with the hands.

gre.s: Contrary to the old belief that the adult brain is fixed, researchers now regard it as remarkably ____, capable of forming new connections throughout life.
gre.clue: capable of forming new connections throughout life

example: Young children's accents are remarkably plastic, so a girl who moves from Sylhet to London at five may soon sound entirely British.

en: To prepare someone or something for action
hook: GRE trick: to PRIME is to PREPARE, like priming a wall before painting.
story: Prime. In the week before Mitu's GRE, her tutor taught her nothing new. Instead, he gave her timed practice sets every morning at the exact hour of the real test, so her brain would be ready to focus at that time. He was priming her: preparing her for action. Painters prime a wall with a base coat before the real colour. Old water pumps must be primed before they work. Synonyms: prepare, ready, groom. Opposite: neglect.

gre.s: Before the negotiations began, the lawyer took care to ____ her client, rehearsing every likely question so that nothing would catch him off guard.
gre.clue: rehearsing every likely question so that nothing would catch him off guard

example: Before the debate, the team captain primed each speaker with the opposing side's strongest arguments and the best replies to them.

en: Favoring drastic change; relating to the fundamental nature of something
hook: RADICAL: down to the ROOT (radix).
story: Radical. For years, a village in Kurigram tried small fixes against flooding: higher plinths, sandbags, better drains. Nothing worked. Then a young engineer proposed something radical: rebuild the whole village on floating platforms that rise with the water. Radical means favouring drastic change, or relating to the fundamental nature of something. It comes from Latin radix, root, as in radish; radical change goes all the way to the roots. Synonyms: drastic, sweeping, fundamental. Opposite: incremental.

gre.s: Rather than tinkering with the existing curriculum, the new principal proposed a ____ overhaul that would reshape every course from the ground up.
gre.clue: reshape every course from the ground up

example: Moving the whole newsroom from print to online publishing in a single year was a radical step for the century-old newspaper.

en: To consider something carefully; to show or express something
hook: REFLECT: like a mirror, turning thoughts back on yourself.
story: Reflect. After failing her first GRE practice test, Joya did not rush to take another. She sat with her score report and reflected. Which questions had she rushed? Which words had she guessed? Slow, careful thought revealed the pattern. Months later, her final score reflected that effort: it showed how much she had grown. To reflect is to think deeply, or to show and reveal, the way a mirror reflects a face. Synonyms: ponder, mirror, indicate.

gre.s: The novel's bleak tone may ____ the author's own despair during the war years, a period she described in her letters as the darkest of her life.
gre.clue: a period she described in her letters as the darkest of her life

example: Rising rents in Dhanmondi reflect the growing demand for apartments near the city's best schools.

en: Unusual enough to be noticed and admired; exceptional
hook: REMARKABLE: worth a REMARK.
story: Remarkable. Mitu's neighbor, a widow who sold vegetables in Karwan Bazar, raised four children alone, saved every spare taka, and sent all four to university. Two of them became doctors. When a local newspaper ran her story, readers called it remarkable: worthy of attention, extraordinary. Remarkable literally means worth remarking on, worth talking about. A remarkable achievement stands out sharply from the ordinary. Synonyms: extraordinary, striking, noteworthy, exceptional.

gre.s: What makes the novel ____ is not its plot, which is entirely conventional, but its narrator, who speaks in a voice unlike any other in modern fiction.
gre.clue: a voice unlike any other in modern fiction

example: The rescued hawk made a remarkable recovery, flying again only three weeks after the vet set its broken wing.

en: Far away; distant; slight or faint
hook: REMOTE: far away like a REMOTE village, or a remote chance.
story: Remote. Sabbir's grandparents live in a remote char village in the middle of the Jamuna, far from any town and reachable only by boat. But on the GRE, remote often has another sense: slight or faint. When Sabbir asked whether the ferry would run during the storm, the boatman laughed. "There is only a remote possibility." Remote can also describe a person who is distant and aloof. Synonyms: distant, isolated; or slight, faint, slim.

gre.s: Although the doctors admitted there was a ____ chance that the experimental treatment would succeed, they warned the family not to raise their hopes.
gre.clue: warned the family not to raise their hopes

example: The odds that the asteroid will strike Earth are remote, but astronomers plan to keep tracking it for the next fifty years.

en: Small or minor (adj.); to insult by ignoring (verb); an insult
hook: GRE trick: SLIGHT as a verb means to snub someone.
story: Slight. At her cousin's wedding, the host greeted every guest warmly at the door: hugs, compliments, questions about their health. When Nadia's mother arrived, he looked straight past her, said nothing, and turned to the next guest. She felt deeply slighted. As a verb, to slight is to insult someone by ignoring them. As an adjective, slight means small: a slight fever, a slight delay. As a noun, a slight is the insult itself.

gre.s: The ambassador was offended by what she regarded as a deliberate ____: she had been seated at the far end of the table, away from every other head of delegation.
gre.clue: seated at the far end of the table, away from every other head of delegation

example: The novelist took it as a slight when her name was left off the festival poster, even though she was its keynote speaker.

en: Based on valid reasoning; in good condition; reliable
hook: GRE trick: SOUND means solid and valid — a sound argument.
story: Sound. Mitu's plan to study abroad impressed her parents: she had savings for the first year, a partial scholarship, a part-time job lined up, and a clear career goal. Her reasoning was sound. Meanwhile, the old bridge outside her village had cracked pillars and was declared structurally unsound. On the GRE, sound means logically valid, solid, or reliable, not just a noise. Sound advice, a sound argument, a sound investment.

gre.s: Although the argument's conclusion was surprising, its reasoning was ____, resting on well-established data and careful logic.
gre.clue: resting on well-established data and careful logic

example: The judge found the engineer's analysis sound and ordered the builder to repair the cracked pillars at his own expense.

en: To originate from; to be caused by
hook: STEM FROM: like a plant's STEM growing from its root.
story: Stem from. Ishita's younger sister was terrified of water and would not go near the pond. Their mother explained that the fear stemmed from an accident: at three, the girl had slipped off a boat and nearly drowned. To stem from is to originate from or be caused by. Picture a stem growing from its roots: the visible problem grows from a hidden source. Do not confuse it with the verb stem, meaning to stop a flow. Synonyms: arise from, derive from.

gre.s: Most of the town's current troubles ____ a single decision made decades ago: closing the factory that once employed half its residents.
gre.clue: a single decision made decades ago

example: Many of the river's pollution problems stem from tanneries upstream that dump untreated waste directly into the water.

en: Not to be trusted; of doubtful quality
hook: GRE trick: SUSPECT as an adjective means questionable.
story: Suspect. A website promised Ishita a full scholarship abroad if she paid a ten-thousand-taka registration fee within twenty-four hours. The site had spelling mistakes, no physical address, and a phone number nobody ever answered. Her professor said the offer was suspect: not to be trusted, of doubtful quality. As an adjective, suspect is stressed on the first syllable and means questionable. Suspect data and suspect motives cannot be relied on. Synonyms: dubious, questionable, fishy.

gre.s: The study's conclusions are ____, since it was funded by the very company whose product it praises and its raw data have never been released.
gre.clue: funded by the very company whose product it praises

example: Curators considered the painting's signature suspect, since the artist had always signed with his initials and never with his full name.

en: Relating to or done by everyone; applicable in all cases
hook: UNIVERSAL: across the whole UNIVERSE.
story: Universal. Over recent decades, Bangladesh worked hard to bring every child into primary school: boys and girls, rich and poor, city and village. Free textbooks, stipends for girls, and schools on remote river islands followed. The goal was universal education: done by or applying to everyone, with no exceptions. Think of the universe, everything there is. A universal truth holds in all cases; universal approval means everyone agrees. Synonyms: general, global, all-embracing. Opposite: particular.

gre.s: The proposal enjoyed nearly ____ support within the committee: of its forty members, only one voted against it.
gre.clue: only one voted against it

example: Gravity is universal, so the same force that pulls a mango from its branch also keeps the moon circling Earth.

en: Lacking; not good enough
hook: GRE trick: FOUND WANTING means found lacking, not desiring.
story: Wanting. Rafi's first research paper had good data, but his professor returned it with a single comment: "The analysis is wanting." Rafi was puzzled at first. Then he understood: wanting here means lacking, not good enough. When something is weighed and found wanting, it falls short of a standard. In older English, want meant lack, as in the proverb: for want of a nail, the shoe was lost. Synonyms: deficient, lacking, inadequate.

gre.s: The proposal was praised for its ambition, but on close examination its financial projections were found ____, resting on assumptions that no serious economist would accept.
gre.clue: resting on assumptions that no serious economist would accept

example: Judged against modern safety codes, the old stadium's fire exits are sadly wanting, so the city has closed the upper stands.
